What would happen if my house caught on fire? "What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?" the author asks. Two summers ago, I asked myself: Wouldn't it suck if my first love met someone unexpectedly and got over me before I could begin to move on? I should've known it would happen, since it happens quite often. My first kiss, who refused to be my boyfriend, met the girl of his dreams while I still ached for him. They're still together today. Since then, I've been the second choice for several more men. The most recent ones occurred this summer, when I tried and failed to win the heart of my friend Ken -- he started dating the person that he truly liked instead of settling for me. I lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend (although, in that case, I think they belonged together anyway). Each time, I laughed one of those sad, desperate guffaws -- here we go again! What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me? Another concept may be more applicable to my situation: the idea of a self-fulfilling prophecy. Perhaps I'm so aware of my "magic touch" that I'm making it happen. While the first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him what may happen. At the time, though, he waved the thought away. "I'm so picky, I rarely really like a girl like I like you," he typed. A month later, he must've been pleasantly shocked to discover my unfortunate power reached across the Atlantic Ocean. When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was angry I'd let this happen to me again. I raged at him. He argued that it's irrational to use my past experience to predict the outcome of my future relationships (or my attempts at them). I'm sure that there'll be a guy someday who doesn't find me easy to move on from, but in the meantime I can't ignore the pattern and pretend that each time was a coincidence, as Ken had wanted me to do. I don't know if there is a way to avoid the seemingly inevitable. Each time I let my hopes conquer my superstition, there's a crash, a burn, a deflation, and the temporary loss of the ability to giggle, but I choose the chance of being the girl before the girlfriend over giving up the chance for breaking my streak. (The Frisky) — There is a school of thought that suggests if you imagine something catastrophic, it will not happen. What if my family died in a car accident? What if my house caught fire? “What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?” the author asks.

Two summers ago, I asked myself: Wouldn’t it be awful if my first love met someone unexpectedly and got over me before I could even begin to move on? Thankfully, my family and my house are safe. My feelings, my love life, and my ego, however, are still in need of repair.

“I met someone.”

The text message appeared on my phone screen, and I stopped walking. A group of friends and I were leaving the movie theater, and it felt as though every feeling he had ever had for me had been erased in a single night. We had broken up because he was studying in Europe. Poignantly, we had expressed our feelings for each other just two nights earlier. Then he became someone else’s boyfriend—and remained so for far longer than he and I had lasted.

I should have known it would happen, because it happens often. My first kiss, who refused to be my boyfriend, met the girl of his dreams while I was still aching for him. They are still together today. Since then, I have been the second choice for several more men. The most recent instances occurred this summer, when I tried and failed to win the heart of my friend Ken; he began dating the person he truly liked instead of settling for me. I also lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend—though, in that case, I think they belonged together anyway.

Each time, I laughed one of those sad, desperate guffaws: Here we go again. What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?

Another concept may be more applicable to my situation: the self-fulfilling prophecy. Perhaps I am so conscious of my “magic touch” that I am helping to make it happen. When my first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him what might occur. At the time, however, he dismissed the idea.

“I’m so picky, I rarely really like a girl the way I like you,” he typed.

A month later, he must have been pleasantly shocked to discover that my unfortunate power extended across the Atlantic Ocean.

When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was angry that I had let this happen to me again. I raged at him. He argued that it was irrational to use my past experiences to predict the outcome of my future relationships—or my attempts at them. I am sure that someday there will be a man who does not find me easy to move on from. In the meantime, however, I cannot ignore the pattern and pretend each instance was merely a coincidence, as Ken wanted me to do.

I do not know whether there is any way to avoid the seemingly inevitable. Each time I allow my hopes to overcome my superstition, there is a crash, a burn, a deflation, and a temporary loss of the ability to giggle. Still, I choose the chance of being the girl before the girlfriend over giving up the possibility of breaking my streak.

(The Frisky) — Some people believe that imagining the worst can somehow prevent it from coming true. What if my family were killed in a car crash? What if my home went up in flames? The writer wonders, “Why do men seem to find the woman they truly want right after there’s a spark with me?”

Two summers ago, I found myself thinking: Wouldn’t it be awful if my first love happened to meet someone new and got over me before I had even started getting over him? Fortunately, my family is fine and my house is still standing. My emotions, romantic life, and pride, however, are still recovering.

“I met someone.”

When that text appeared on my phone, I froze mid-step. I was leaving the movie theater with a group of friends, and it felt as though every feeling he’d had for me had been erased overnight. We had ended things because he was going to study in Europe. In a cruelly poetic twist, we had told each other how we felt only two nights earlier. Then he became another girl’s boyfriend—and stayed with her far longer than he and I had ever lasted.

I probably should have expected it, because this kind of thing has happened to me repeatedly. My first kiss, who wouldn’t agree to be my boyfriend, found the love of his life while I was still hurting over him. They’re still together now. After that, I became the runner-up for several other men.

The latest examples happened this summer. I tried—and failed—to make my friend Ken fall for me; instead, he began dating the woman he actually wanted, rather than choosing me as a fallback. I also lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend, though in that situation I suspect they were meant to be together anyway. Every time, I let out the same bleak, helpless laugh: here we go again.

Why is it that after a man has chemistry with me, he seems to end up bonding with the woman he really wants?

Maybe another explanation fits better: the self-fulfilling prophecy. Maybe I am so conscious of my so-called “magic touch” that I somehow help bring it about. When my first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him that this could happen. At the time, he dismissed the idea.

“I’m so picky, I almost never like a girl the way I like you,” he wrote.

A month later, he must have been surprised to learn that my unlucky talent could apparently work across the Atlantic.

When Ken told me he was seeing Mary, I was furious with myself for letting the same pattern happen again. I lashed out at him. He told me it was unreasonable to use my past experiences to forecast what would happen in future relationships—or attempts at relationships. I’m sure that someday there will be a man who won’t find it so easy to move on from me. But until then, I can’t simply ignore the repetition and pretend every instance was a coincidence, the way Ken wanted me to.

I don’t know whether there’s any way to escape what feels unavoidable. Whenever I allow hope to overpower my superstition, everything ends in collapse, disappointment, humiliation, and a temporary inability to laugh. Still, I would rather risk being the woman who comes before the girlfriend than give up the possibility of finally breaking the pattern.

By anticipating catastrophe, she feels as though she is protecting herself from it, as if fear itself could serve as a kind of charm against disappointment.

She remembers one of the earliest and most painful instances of this pattern: her first love, who went away to study in Europe and later told her that he had met someone else. The news devastated her. What had once seemed intimate and certain suddenly became proof that she could be replaced, and that the person she wanted most might ultimately choose another woman.

Over time, she begins to recognize a recurring pattern in her romantic life. Again and again, the men she likes seem to move on from her to women they truly desire. She comes to see herself as a temporary figure in their lives, someone they pass through on the way to the person they really want. This sense of being provisional, of never being the final choice, becomes a painful theme.

To support this feeling, she recalls several examples. There was her first kiss, which did not lead to the romantic significance she may have hoped for. There was her friend Ken, whose attention or affection did not ultimately become the kind of love she wanted. There was Brian, another example of someone who seemed to confirm the same pattern. Each memory adds to her impression that she is not chosen fully, but instead occupies the role of second choice, rehearsal, or placeholder.

By the end of the reflection, the author begins to question whether her belief has shaped her reality. If she expects to be passed over, does she behave in ways that make it more likely? Has her fear of abandonment become a self-fulfilling prophecy? Rather than offering a simple answer, she lingers in that uncertainty, examining the possibility that her anticipation of loss may not protect her from pain, but may instead help reproduce the very disappointments she dreads.

For a long time, I thought there was something almost supernatural about my dating life. The pattern was so consistent that it began to feel less like coincidence and more like a role I had been assigned without my consent: I would meet a man, connect with him, share something warm or flirtatious or emotionally intimate, and then, not long afterward, he would find someone else. Not just casually date someone else, but settle down. Commit. Become serious. Become the kind of partner I had quietly hoped he might become with me.

At first, I treated it like a cruel joke. I would tell friends, half-laughing and half-wounded, that I was some kind of romantic good-luck charm for men. Spend a little time with me, open up to me, let me believe there might be something there, and suddenly the next woman you meet becomes the love of your life. I was the woman before the woman. The emotional rehearsal. The almost. The person who helped someone become ready, only to watch him choose somebody else.

There were enough examples to make the theory feel convincing. One man I had been talking to for weeks disappeared into vague replies and “busy” excuses, only for me to learn later that he had started a serious relationship almost immediately afterward. Another had leaned on me during a lonely period, sharing fears, dreams, and late-night confessions, then gently told me he “wasn’t in the right place for anything real.” A month later, he was in a relationship that looked very real. There were others too: men who seemed uncertain with me but suddenly certain with someone else, men who claimed not to be ready until, apparently, they were.

Each time it happened, I felt the same familiar sting. It was not only jealousy, though jealousy was there. It was humiliation. It was the feeling of having been considered and quietly rejected, of being good enough to comfort, excite, entertain, or prepare someone, but not good enough to be chosen. I began to think of myself as a second choice before anyone had even made a decision.

That phrase—second choice—became painfully powerful. Once it entered my mind, it colored everything. If a man took too long to respond, I assumed he was more interested in someone else. If he complimented me, I wondered whether he meant it or whether I was simply convenient. If he hesitated, I heard rejection before he had said a word. I was no longer just experiencing disappointment; I was anticipating it, bracing for it, almost waiting for it to prove me right.

Eventually, I started to wonder whether the pattern was not only something happening to me, but something I was helping to create. Not intentionally, of course. I was not choosing pain. I was not asking to be overlooked. But the idea of a self-fulfilling prophecy began to make uncomfortable sense. If I believed, deep down, that I would not be chosen, then perhaps I acted from that belief in ways I did not fully notice.

Maybe I accepted uncertainty for too long because it felt familiar. Maybe I gave too much emotional intimacy to men who had not earned it because I wanted to prove my value. Maybe I became so afraid of seeming demanding that I never asked clearly for what I wanted. Maybe my fear of being second made me behave like someone already defeated, someone waiting to be replaced rather than someone expecting to be loved.

That realization did not make the pain disappear. In some ways, it made it more complicated. It is easier to believe in a curse than to admit that your expectations may be shaping your choices. A curse lets you remain innocent. A pattern asks you to look more closely. It asks what you tolerate, what you ignore, what stories you tell yourself before anyone else has had the chance to speak.

Still, I do not think the answer is to blame myself. The men who were careless with my feelings were responsible for their part. Mixed signals are real. Emotional unavailability is real. Some people do use others as bridges between loneliness and commitment. But I am beginning to see that my own fear may have made me especially vulnerable to that kind of dynamic. When you expect to be the temporary person, you may overlook the signs that someone is treating you temporarily. When you believe you are destined to be second, you may forget to insist on being met as a first choice from the beginning.

The strange thing about this pattern is that it became predictable, and predictability can feel like proof. Each new disappointment seemed to confirm what I already believed about myself: that I was the person men passed through on their way to someone better. But maybe what it really confirmed was that I had learned to recognize love through absence, uncertainty, and waiting. Maybe I had mistaken anxiety for intuition.

I am trying now to imagine a different story. One in which I do not enter every connection already preparing to lose. One in which I pay attention not only to whether someone likes me, but to whether he is available, consistent, and capable of choosing me openly. One in which I do not audition for love or accept the role of almost-loved simply because it is familiar.

Perhaps the pattern was never magic. Perhaps I was not a curse, a stepping stone, or a romantic good-luck charm for other women. Perhaps I was simply afraid, and that fear taught me to expect less than I wanted. And perhaps the first step toward changing the ending is to stop walking into every beginning convinced that I already know how it will end.

counterfactuals.output:
**CNN —** I first noticed it after Mark.

He was the kind of guy who texted in full sentences, remembered my coffee order, and once told me, with alarming sincerity, that he “wasn’t sure he believed in timing.” We went on three dates, kissed once outside a bar with sticky floors, and then he vanished into the polite fog where almost-relationships go to die.

Two weeks later, he posted a photo with her: glowing, hiking, matching fleece zip-ups. Six months after that, they were engaged.

At first, I blamed bad luck. Then came Daniel, who flirted with me all summer and introduced his “soulmate” by Labor Day. Then Chris, who took me to dinner, said he was “not looking for anything serious,” and promptly moved in with a woman who owned a sourdough starter and a golden retriever.

Eventually, I began to suspect I had a gift.

Not the useful kind, like being able to parallel park under pressure or remember passwords. No, my apparent superpower was this: any man who showed interest in me would immediately be rerouted by the universe to the woman he was actually supposed to marry.

I wasn’t a girlfriend. I was a romantic layover. A human airport lounge with decent lighting.

My friends tried to comfort me. “Maybe you’re helping them become emotionally available,” one said, which sounded less like reassurance and more like unpaid labor. Another suggested I was “good luck,” as if I were a rabbit’s foot with bangs.

But after a while, it was hard not to see the pattern. I would laugh at a man’s jokes, let myself imagine a future involving brunch, and then — poof — he’d meet a woman who did hot yoga, worked in nonprofit development, and looked incredible in overalls.

I started calling it my magic touch.

And like most magic, it was only impressive if you weren’t the one disappearing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an article in the voice of The Frisky about being “the girl before the girlfriend,” including examples involving a first love in Europe, a first kiss, and friends named Ken, Brian, and Mary.
counterfactuals.output:
## The Girl Before the Girlfriend

There is a very specific, very maddening kind of romantic supporting character, and some of us have played her more times than we’d like to admit: **the girl before the girlfriend**.

You are not the ex. You are not the girlfriend. You are not even always the almost-girlfriend, which at least sounds poetic and tortured enough to justify three glasses of wine and a group text. No, you are the emotional warm-up act. The soft launch. The romantic palate cleanser. The woman who arrives just before a man suddenly becomes “ready” for someone else.

You know the one.

He tells you he’s not looking for anything serious. He says he’s complicated. He says timing is weird. He says he just got out of something. He says he’s “figuring himself out,” which is often code for “I would like girlfriend-level comfort without girlfriend-level accountability.”

And then, two months after things fizzle with you, he is on Instagram in matching sweaters with a woman named Caitlin, captioning photos, “When you know, you know.”

Excuse me, sir. Apparently what you knew was how to use me as an emotional IKEA instruction manual.

Being the girl before the girlfriend is especially infuriating because you can see the transformation happen in real time. With you, he was vague about dinner plans. With her, he makes reservations. With you, he “wasn’t big on labels.” With her, he is in her family’s Christmas card. With you, he needed space. With her, he adopts a rescue dog and learns the word “we.”

I have been this girl. More than once. Which is either tragic or an impressive commitment to field research.

There was my first love in Europe, because of course there was. If you are going to get emotionally demolished, I do recommend doing it somewhere with cobblestones and cheap wine. He had a beautiful accent, a face like a statue, and the emotional availability of a locked museum after hours. He told me he loved me in a train station, because Europe is rude like that. Everything becomes cinematic even when someone is actively ruining your life.

We wrote letters. We kissed under old buildings. I convinced myself geography was the villain, not the fact that he could only adore me when I was leaving. For months, he told me he couldn’t possibly have a real relationship. Too much distance. Too much uncertainty. Too much “life.”

Then, shortly after I went home, he got a girlfriend.

A local one, naturally.

She got the boyfriend version of him: present, stable, smiling in photos at outdoor markets. I got the limited-edition travel romance version, all longing and no follow-through. I was the beautifully lit prologue to somebody else’s chapter one.

And then there was the first kiss.

Not my first kiss ever, but the first kiss that made me feel like I had been personally selected by fate, hormones, and whatever perfume sample I was wearing at the time. He was funny and nervous and leaned in like it mattered. Afterward, I did what any dignified woman would do: I replayed it in my mind approximately 4,000 times and told my friends it was “probably nothing” while behaving like it was the opening scene of a biopic.

He told me he wasn’t ready. He told me he liked me too much to mess it up. Please note: “I like you too much to date you” should be illegal in at least 37 states.

A month later, he was dating someone else. Not just dating — thriving. Picnics. Brunch. Couple Halloween costume. The works.

I asked my friend Ken what this meant, because Ken is one of those men who can translate male nonsense into regular human language.

Ken shrugged and said, “Maybe you made him realize he wanted a relationship.”

“Great,” I said. “So I’m a romantic multivitamin?”

Brian, who is less diplomatic and more likely to say the thing everyone else is avoiding, put it differently: “You’re like the tutorial level.”

Thank you, Brian. Very healing.

Mary, who is wise in the way only a woman who has deleted and re-downloaded dating apps with full spiritual awareness can be, said, “No. You’re not the tutorial level. You’re just meeting men while they’re still under construction.”

That sounded better. Still annoying, but better.

Because here’s the thing: being the girl before the girlfriend can make you feel like you were almost enough. Like if you had been more patient, more mysterious, more chill, less chill, hotter, softer, busier, more available, better at texting, worse at texting, somehow you would have unlocked the final version of him.

But that is a scam. A very popular scam, but a scam nonetheless.

Sometimes people become ready because of you. Sometimes they become ready after you. Sometimes they were ready the whole time, just not with you, which is brutal but useful information. And sometimes they are not “ready” at all — they just found someone whose needs, timing, and tolerance for their nonsense happened to align.

None of this means you were deficient. It means you were present for a transition you did not get to benefit from.

The girl before the girlfriend often does invisible labor. She listens. She reassures. She teaches him that vulnerability won’t kill him. She reminds him how to flirt. She helps him remember he is capable of wanting something. She is the one who hears, “I’ve never told anyone this before,” only to watch him tell the next woman, “I’m really working on being emotionally open.”

Sir, I know. I held the flashlight.

The danger is that you start mistaking this role for your identity. You begin to believe you are the woman men practice on, not the woman they choose. You look at every new connection like it comes with a countdown clock. You wonder if you are simply the romantic equivalent of spring training.

But you are not a waiting room. You are not a rehab center for men with intimacy issues. You are not a charming anecdote he tells his future girlfriend about “this girl I once knew.”

You are the main event, even if someone else failed to notice.

The trick is learning to spot the pattern earlier. When a man says he doesn’t know what he wants, believe him. When he says he can’t give you what you need, don’t hear that as a challenge. When he treats your patience like an all-access pass, revoke it. When the relationship exists mostly in potential, fantasy, or late-night conversations that never become daylight plans, ask yourself if you are being loved or merely auditioned.

And if you discover, once again, that you were the girl before the girlfriend? Be annoyed. Be petty for one evening. Send screenshots to Mary. Let Ken say something sensible and Brian say something offensive but accurate. Mourn the version of the story you thought you were in.

Then remember: the fact that someone became better after you does not mean you were meant to settle for the rough draft.

Let him be someone else’s boyfriend.

You go find the man who does not need a prequel to know you’re the plot.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Recreate a 2009 syndicated women’s lifestyle article excerpt that starts with “There exists a school of thought…” and explores superstition, self-fulfilling prophecy, and repeated romantic rejection.
counterfactuals.output:
Sorry, I can’t recreate or provide a copyrighted article excerpt based on its opening line.

I can help in either of these ways:

**Brief summary of the likely themes:**  
The excerpt appears to discuss how superstition and expectation can shape romantic outcomes—especially when someone experiences repeated rejection. It likely connects the idea of a self-fulfilling prophecy to dating: if a person believes they are unlucky in love or destined to be rejected, that belief may influence their behavior, confidence, and choices in ways that make rejection more likely.

**Original passage in a similar broad theme:**  
There’s a strange comfort in believing love follows a pattern, even when the pattern hurts. After enough disappointments, a person can begin to treat rejection not as an event but as evidence—proof that some invisible rule is at work. Superstition steps in where confidence has worn thin: the wrong dress, the wrong day, the wrong kind of man, the same doomed ending.

But the danger of believing in romantic bad luck is that belief can quietly become behavior. Expecting to be dismissed, someone may pull back too soon, test too often, or read indifference into ordinary silences. What looks like fate may, in part, be fear rehearsing the ending before the story has had a chance to begin.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person relationship essay framed as a news/lifestyle piece with “(The Frisky) --” at the beginning, where the author asks why men connect with their dream girl after sparking with her.
counterfactuals.output:
(The Frisky) -- The first time I met him, there was that unmistakable spark — the kind that makes a crowded room go quiet, even if only in your own head.

We talked too long, laughed too easily, and fell into the kind of rhythm that makes you wonder if chemistry is less a mystery and more a physical fact. By the end of the night, I was doing the thing I always tell myself not to do: imagining the next conversation, the next date, the next version of myself reflected in someone else’s interest.

And then, almost immediately, I had the question so many women have asked over brunch, over text, and while staring too hard at an unread message: Why do men connect so intensely with their “dream girl” after the spark — and then sometimes seem completely unprepared for what comes next?

It’s a strange modern dating contradiction. A man can pursue you with the confidence of someone who knows exactly what he wants. He can say you’re different, say he’s never felt this kind of ease before, say the timing feels almost suspiciously perfect. He can lean into the spark as if it’s a sign.

But connection, I’ve learned, is not the same thing as readiness.

For a long time, I confused chemistry with clarity. If a man lit up around me, I assumed he understood what that meant. If he called me his dream girl, I assumed he was prepared to wake up and actually know me in daylight — not just in the flattering glow of flirtation, possibility, and projection.

But a “dream girl” is often not a woman at all. She is an idea.

She is what a man thinks love will feel like when it finally arrives without complications. She is beautiful timing, emotional rescue, proof that he is capable of wanting something real. She is the answer to loneliness, boredom, heartbreak, or the fear that life has become too ordinary.

And then she becomes human.

She has needs. She has questions. She has a past, preferences, fears, bad moods, boundaries, and a calendar. She wants consistency, not just intensity. She wants to know whether the spark is being tended or merely admired.

That, I think, is where many men panic.

The spark is easy to romanticize because it asks very little of anyone at first. It’s all sensation: attraction, novelty, curiosity, the thrill of being seen. Real connection asks for more. It requires emotional stamina. It asks a person to stay present after the chase slows down, after the mystery becomes familiarity, after the “dream” starts requiring communication.

I don’t think men are alone in this. Women do it too. I have certainly fallen for the idea of someone before I fully understood the person. I have mistaken potential for compatibility. I have treated a spark like evidence when it was only an invitation.

But I do think some men are especially skilled at pursuing the feeling of a dream woman while being less equipped to build a relationship with the real one.

Maybe it’s because men are often taught to hunt for love more than inhabit it. They are encouraged to win the girl, impress the girl, desire the girl — but not always to sit across from her and be vulnerable, accountable, and emotionally specific. So when a woman feels rare, they move toward her. When she asks to be met in reality, they hesitate.

I used to take that hesitation personally. I wondered if I had done something wrong, revealed too much, expected too much, become too available or not available enough. I ran the usual exhausting diagnostics: Was I too intense? Too guarded? Too honest? Too optimistic?

Now I think the better question is not, “Why did he spark with me and then struggle?”

It’s, “Can he turn attraction into action?”

Because that is the test. Not whether he feels something. Not whether he says I’m unlike anyone he’s met. Not whether the first night feels like a movie scene. The test is whether he can follow through after the feeling arrives.

A man who truly connects with his dream girl has to do more than recognize her. He has to choose her in practical, repeated ways. He has to let the fantasy mature into intimacy. He has to be curious about who she is, not just grateful for how she makes him feel.

And the woman — me, in this case — has to resist auditioning for the role of someone’s perfect answer.

I no longer want to be a dream girl if that means being placed on a pedestal too high for real life. I don’t want to be the spark someone remembers fondly while failing to build a fire. I want to be met, not imagined. Chosen, not idealized. Loved in the ordinary moments after the chemistry announces itself and the real work begins.

So why do men connect with their dream girl after sparking with her?

Maybe because sparks are powerful. Maybe because some people recognize possibility before they understand responsibility. Maybe because attraction can open a door that emotional readiness still has to walk through.

The spark matters. I won’t pretend it doesn’t.

But the older I get, the more I trust what happens afterward.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a full article-style passage about a woman noticing a pattern that every man she falls for quickly chooses someone else, ending with her deciding to keep risking heartbreak rather than give up on love.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Pattern She Couldn’t Stop Seeing**

At first, she told herself it was coincidence.

One man reconnected with an ex two weeks after he stopped calling. Another announced, with a strange kind of apologetic joy, that he had “unexpectedly met someone.” A third had spent months trading late-night messages with her, sharing fears and childhood stories and songs that felt too personal to be casual—only to appear in photographs soon after with another woman, smiling in a way she had once imagined was reserved for her.

Individually, each disappointment had an explanation. Timing. Confusion. Emotional unavailability. Bad luck. Modern dating, with all its half-promises and unfinished conversations.

But after a while, the separate incidents began to arrange themselves into a pattern she could not ignore: every time she fell for a man, he seemed to choose someone else almost immediately afterward.

It was not always cruel. In fact, that made it harder. These men were rarely villains. They did not always lie, manipulate, or make grand promises they never intended to keep. Sometimes they liked her. Sometimes they admired her. Sometimes they even seemed to hover at the edge of loving her, close enough that she could feel the warmth of possibility.

And then, suddenly, they were gone.

Not gone into loneliness. Not gone to find themselves. Gone into someone else’s arms.

She began to wonder what role she was playing in their lives. Was she the woman men met right before they were ready? The one who helped them remember how to be tender, only for them to offer that tenderness elsewhere? Was she a bridge, a rehearsal, a waiting room?

The thought embarrassed her. She hated the bitterness of it. She did not want to become someone who measured her worth by being chosen, did not want to reduce love to a competition she kept losing. Yet the ache was real. So was the humiliation of hoping, again and again, and watching that hope become proof of her own vulnerability.

Friends tried to comfort her.

“It’s not about you,” they said.

And perhaps they were right. Perhaps attraction is not a verdict. Perhaps one person’s choice of someone else does not make the unchosen person less beautiful, less intelligent, less deserving. The heart is not a courtroom. Love is not always fair, and it is not always logical.

Still, it felt personal because she was the one left carrying it.

She replayed conversations, searching for the moment everything shifted. Had she cared too much? Said too little? Been too available, too guarded, too serious, too careful? She examined herself until self-awareness became a form of punishment.

There were days she promised herself she was finished. She would stop reading meaning into kindness. She would stop staying up late for men who had not earned her sleeplessness. She would stop imagining futures from fragments. She would become practical, contained, untouchable.

For a while, she succeeded.

She filled her evenings. She answered messages slowly. She trained herself not to expect anything from anyone. She wore independence like armor and told herself peace was better than longing.

And it was—sometimes.

There was comfort in not waiting for a name to appear on her phone. There was dignity in refusing to chase unclear affection. There was strength in learning that disappointment would not destroy her.

But beneath all that strength, something remained alive.

She still noticed tenderness. She still felt her heart lift at the sound of a laugh that met hers in the same rhythm. She still believed in the strange electricity of being understood. Despite everything, love had not become ridiculous to her. Wounded, yes. Risky, yes. But not ridiculous.

That was the truth she eventually had to face: she did not want a life built only around avoiding pain.

Avoiding heartbreak might keep her safe, but it would also require her to close the very part of herself she liked most—the part that could hope, soften, imagine, and reach. The part that still believed connection was worth the danger of loss.

So she stopped treating her past as a prophecy.

Maybe another man would choose someone else. Maybe she would misread another moment. Maybe she would again feel the sharp, familiar sting of being almost loved. But maybe, one day, someone would stay. Maybe someone would not need to lose her in order to know what he had found. Maybe the pattern was not fate, but merely history.

And history, she reminded herself, is not the same as destiny.

She did not become reckless. She did not decide to hand her heart to anyone who smiled at her kindly. She learned to move more slowly, to watch actions instead of possibilities, to listen when uncertainty spoke louder than affection. She learned that risking love did not mean abandoning herself.

But she also refused to surrender to fear.

In the end, she chose the braver heartbreak over the quieter emptiness. She chose to remain open, not because love had been easy, but because it still mattered to her. She chose to believe that being passed over did not make her unworthy, and that every ending had not been evidence against her.

She would keep risking it—the awkward beginnings, the fragile hope, the chance of disappointment.

Not because she enjoyed pain.

Not because she had learned nothing.

But because giving up on love would have broken something in her more deeply than heartbreak ever had.
